hints: Start by thinking why the carbonyl carbon in propanone is attacked. Consider how oxygen pulls electrons away from carbon.
Think about where the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ goes first, and what must happen to the $\text{C=O}$ double bond at the same time.
After the first attack, consider what type of ion is left on oxygen and how it can become an $\text{OH}$ group using $\text{HCN}$ as a proton source.
walkthrough:
Make the carbonyl polar first**
Picture $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$. Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so the $\text{C=O}$ bond is polar with $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Show this dipole on your diagram. This explains why a nucleophile is attracted to carbon, not oxygen.

Attack by cyanide and break the pi bond**
The carbon in $\text{:CN}^{-}$ has a lone pair and a negative charge, so it is a strong nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting from that lone pair and pointing to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of the carbonyl. At the same time, the pi electrons of $\text{C=O}$ must move away, so draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ bond onto oxygen. This gives the alkoxide intermediate $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(CN)O}^{-}$.

Protonate the alkoxide to finish**
The $\text{O}^{-}$ is strongly basic. It takes $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{HCN}$ (which reforms $\text{CN}^{-}$). Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to an $\text{H}^{+}$. This forms the $\text{OH}$ group of the cyanohydrin A, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(OH)CN}$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\delta+$ on carbonyl C, $\delta-$ on carbonyl O, curly arrow from lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ to carbonyl C, curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O.
Step 2: intermediate $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(CN)O}^{-}$.
Step 3: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ (from $\text{HCN}$) to give A.

hints: Look closely at the central carbon in A and list the four groups attached to it to see if any are repeated.
walkthrough:
Test for a chiral centre**
For optical isomerism you need a carbon with four different groups attached. Look at the central C in A: it is bonded to $\text{OH}$, to $\text{CN}$, and to two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups. Because two groups are identical methyl groups, this carbon is not chiral, so no non-superimposable mirror images exist.
Final answer: The central carbon in A is not bonded to four different atoms or groups (it has two identical $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups), so A is not chiral and shows no optical isomerism.

hints: Focus on what changes from A to B. The $\text{CN}$ group becomes $\text{COOH}$, think which type of hydrolysis does this.
walkthrough:
Recognise nitrile to acid**
Going from $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(OH)CN}$ to $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C(OH)COOH}$ is hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid. This needs aqueous acid and heat. Either $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$ heated under reflux works.
Final answer: Heat with dilute aqueous acid, e.g. $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$, with heating.

hints: Compare propanone $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$ with product C $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$ and count how many extra H atoms are needed.
walkthrough:
Balance H for ketone to alcohol**
Propanone has formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}$ and propan-2-ol is $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$. The difference is two hydrogen atoms. Using $[\text{H}]$ to represent hydrogen from the reducing agent: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$$

hints: Identify the longest chain and the position of the $\text{OH}$ group in structure C.
walkthrough:
Name the secondary alcohol**
Structure C is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$ with three carbons and $\text{OH}$ on the middle carbon. That is propan-2-ol.

hints: Recall the visual result when any aldehyde or ketone reacts with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent.
walkthrough:
Recall the positive carbonyl test**
2,4-DNPH reacts with the $\text{C=O}$ in propanone to form a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. The observation is a bright orange, red or yellow precipitate.
Final answer: Orange / red / yellow precipitate.

hints: Think about what Fehling's solution does as an oxidising agent and why ketones resist this change.
walkthrough:
Link oxidising strength to structure**
Fehling's solution is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes but not ketones. Propanone has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and its $\text{C-C}$ bonds are not easily broken under these conditions, so no reaction occurs and the solution stays blue.
Final answer: Fehling's solution cannot oxidise ketones / propanone is not easily oxidised.

hints: Check Table 4.1 for the bond that absorbs at 2850-2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and see which of A, B and C all contain that bond.
walkthrough:
Spot the shared absorption**
Table 4.1 shows 2850-2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C-H}$ stretch for alkanes. Look at the structures: A has two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, B has two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, C has $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}$ groups. Because every compound contains $\text{C-H}$ bonds, this peak appears in all spectra and cannot distinguish them.
Final answer: All three compounds A, B and C contain $\text{C-H}$ / $\text{CH}$ bonds (alkane groups), so all show absorption at 2850-2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.

hints: Look for a sharp peak in Fig. 4.3 near 2200 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and match it to Table 4.1 to see which functional group is unique to one compound.
walkthrough:
Use the unique peak to identify**
Fig. 4.3 shows a sharp absorption at about 2200 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Table 4.1 tells you 2200-2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ stretch of a nitrile. Only compound A contains a $\text{CN}$ group, B has $\text{COOH}$ and C has only $\text{C-C}$, $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$. So the spectrum must be A.
Final answer: Compound A, absorption at 2200-2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ indicates $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ (nitrile) which is only present in A.
